name: Veli Bej Bath
description: A small Ottoman bath of the 1570s, set inside the grounds of a hospital in Buda's 2nd district. A central dome sits over an octagonal pool, the Hospitaller order restored it in the early 2010s, and archaeological finds from the work are on display. It is among the few Ottoman baths in Budapest still in use.

children.text: The Veli Bej Bath is a historic Ottoman thermal bath in Budapest's 2nd district, in the Felhévíz area below Rózsadomb. According to Budapest by Locals it was built in 1574-75 by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha, a builder and year the Hospitaller order's own history page also gives, while another Hungarian local-history page says it was completed between 1570 and 1572. Budapest by Locals adds that it survived the recapture of Buda in 1686. The same source calls it the oldest and most beautiful Ottoman bath in Budapest, a superlative that sits uneasily with the Rudas Bath, which Wikipedia dates to 1571 or 1572. A commemorative plaque from its construction is said to remain on a wall.

The building has been changed more than once. In 1806 István Marczibányi handed the bath to the Ordo Hospitalarius, the Hospitaller order that runs the neighbouring hospital; the order's own history page speaks of a gift, while another local-history page says he bought it and passed on the right to run it. A reconstruction led by József Hild in the early 1840s enlarged it and renamed it Kaiser Bad, or Császár Fürdő; the Hospitaller order's history page says only early 1840s, while other sources give 1841-44, 1841-45, 1841-48 or 1842. In the 1970s a modern hospital wing was built around the small bath, which is why it is hard to see from the street.

The order later restored the bath with the help of archaeologists and art historians. Sources give 2011 as the completion of the work, while an article from 2018 says it reopened in 2012. Four smaller domed buildings surround a central cupola, and the main pool is octagonal under a traditional Ottoman dome, with four smaller pools around it. Original Ottoman clay pipes found during the work were preserved and can be seen between the pools and the saunas, and a small display holds finds from the excavation.

Modern wellness areas, including saunas and a jacuzzi, were added to the historic core. The bath is run with the hospital, and the sources say admission is regulated, including a limited capacity and an age limit, so check directly before travelling. Its address is Árpád fejedelem útja 7, close to the Margaret Bridge's Buda end, and it sits in the same area as the Lukács and Császár-Komjádi baths.
Good to know
Budapest by Locals gives trams 4 or 6 to Margit híd Budai hídfő, or trams 17, 19 and 41 to Komjádi Béla utca, as ways to get there.
Admission is regulated, including capacity and age limits, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and rules before going.
Look for the preserved Ottoman clay pipes and the small display of archaeological finds.

historyIntro: The Veli Bej Bath is an Ottoman bath of the 1570s that survived the end of Ottoman rule, passed to a Hospitaller order and was restored in the early 2010s. It now sits inside a hospital complex.

children.text: Budapest by Locals states that the oldest part of the Császár spa, the Turkish bath, was built by Sokollu Mustafa Pasha in 1574-75, and that it survived the recapture of Buda in 1686. The Hospitaller order's own history page gives the same builder and the deciphered year 1574-75, while another Hungarian local-history page dates the work to 1570-1572. The page notes that Buda had roughly seven to nine baths during the 150 years of Ottoman rule and that several of the smaller ones did not survive. Another article reports that a commemorative plaque from the building of the bath remains on a wall.

In 1806 István Marczibányi handed the bath complex to the Ordo Hospitalarius, the Hospitaller order, which expanded the original Ottoman buildings. A reconstruction led by József Hild in the early 1840s enlarged the complex considerably and renamed it Kaiser Bad, or Császár Fürdő; sources date it variously between 1841 and 1848. A 2018 article dates the Hild reconstruction to 1842 and describes the result as classicist. That article adds that in the 1970s the neighbouring hospital was extended with a modern wing that now encloses the small bath, which makes it hard to see from outside.

The Hospitaller order decided to restore the complex fully and to rebuild the original Ottoman bath, working with archaeologists and art historians. Budapest by Locals says the renovation was finished in 2011, while an article published in 2018 says the bath reopened in 2012, so the sources differ by a year. Original clay pipes laid by the Ottomans were found during the work, and archaeologists had them preserved so that they can be seen between the pools and the saunas. A small display of finds, including floor coverings, dishes and grindstones, was also assembled.

name: Aquaworld Resort Budapest
description: A large indoor water park and hotel complex in northern Budapest that opened in December 2008 under a Ramada name. A glass dome 73 metres wide covers the leisure area, which has eleven slides, a wave pool and a surf pool. Check its current name and operator before travelling.

children.text: Aquaworld Resort Budapest is a water park and hotel resort in northern Budapest, built around a leisure area under a glass dome. A trade news item from the waterpark supplier Polin says the complex opened in December 2008 as the Ramada Resort - Aquaworld Budapest and calls it Central Europe's largest indoor water theme park. The dome is described as 73 metres wide and 21 metres high.

The same report says the complex included a 261-room hotel and a separate building with 48 apartments. The water park's attractions include a wave pool, a surf pool, a 180-metre mountain river and eleven water slides that together are almost one kilometre long. Six giant slides start from a slide tower next to the dome, reached by a glass lift or stairs, and the highest rides begin from 17 metres up, and a conveyor-type lift returns the tubes to the start. A children's wing has pools of different depths, slides and a playhouse.

A later travel guide describes the resort as one of Europe's largest indoor water theme parks, with a four-star superior hotel, an Oriental Spa and a separate Sauna World. It notes that some outdoor pools are seasonal. The guides disagree on the number of pools: the opening report counts 21, while the later guide gives 17 in one place and 15 in another, so treat any single figure with caution.

The resort lies far from the city centre. The travel guide says public transport is possible but can be tricky, naming buses 30 and 230 from Keleti Railway Station or Heroes' Square, and also mentions a shuttle from Heroes' Square. Because names, operators and arrangements can change, check the official site for the current operating details.
Good to know
A travel guide lists buses 30 and 230 from Keleti Railway Station or Heroes' Square, and also mentions a shuttle from Heroes' Square, so check the current timetable first.
Slides have height and equipment rules, and some areas such as Sauna World are sold separately, so read the official rules before booking.
Pool counts differ between sources, so check the official site for the current attractions, opening times and tickets.

historyIntro: Aquaworld is a recent attraction, not a historic one: it opened in December 2008 as a water park and hotel complex. The sources read describe its opening and construction, and say little about the years since.

children.text: A report from the water-park supplier Polin says the complex opened in December 2008 as the Ramada Resort - Aquaworld Budapest and describes it as Central Europe's largest indoor water theme park. The hotel had 261 rooms, with a separate building holding 48 apartments, and the leisure area was covered by a glass dome 73 metres wide and 21 metres high. The same report says the water park had 21 pools with a combined surface of 3,300 square metres, a figure that later travel guides do not repeat.

The project manager was the company Eleven Kft, which chose Polin Waterparks and Pool Systems to supply the water park, slides, amusement elements and water engineering. The park has eleven slides with a total length of almost one kilometre, and six giant slides start from a slide tower next to the dome that is reached by a glass lift or by stairs, and the highest ride begins from 17 metres up. A conveyor-type lift carries the tubes back to the start. A later travel guide describes the resort as one of Europe's largest indoor water theme parks and still lists eleven slides, but gives different pool counts of 17 and 15, so the sources about the layout are not fully consistent.

name: Lupa Beach
description: A sandy beach resort on Lupa Lake, a former quarry in Budakalász, just north of the Budapest city limits. It was developed by Sziget Festival founder Károly Gerendai, who opened it in 2016. The lakeside setting includes watersports and play areas and is seasonal.

children.text: Lupa Beach lies on Lake Lupa, in Budakalász, just north of the Budapest city limits. Just Budapest describes the lake as a former quarry transformed into a recreational site, and XpatLoop, writing in 2016, called it a former quarry on the city's northern outskirts where swimming had previously been banned. It is a seasonal destination, so check when it is operating before planning a trip.

The developer was Károly Gerendai, founder of the Sziget Festival. XpatLoop reported that the resort was due to open officially on the evening of 14 July 2016, and that Gerendai described that first summer as a test period to gain experience for the next year. He is reported to have signed a 20-year lease with an option to buy, and as at Sziget the catering and other services were contracted out.

In 2017 the beach was reopened on a larger scale. We Love Budapest reported that the swimmable shoreline had been quadrupled, making the beach about 2.5 kilometres long, and Just Budapest credits Gerendai with the 2017 development. The facilities listed by Just Budapest include a wakeboard centre, kayaking, stand-up paddleboarding, diving, beach volleyball, football, a street-workout park, a children's pool, playgrounds, an inflatable water park and a promenade of food stalls, with accessible pathways.

To get there, Just Budapest suggests the HÉV suburban railway from Batthyány tér toward Budakalász, followed by a walk of about twenty minutes, and says an electric minibus runs from the station to the beach. We Love Budapest names the Budakalász-Lenfonó stop and a summer beach bus. Driving is possible via road 11 toward Szentendre.
Good to know
Take the HÉV from Batthyány tér toward Budakalász and walk about twenty minutes, or look for the shuttle that Just Budapest says serves the beach.
Lupa Beach is seasonal and outside central Budapest, so check the official site for operating dates, opening times and tickets.
Sources name different HÉV stops (Budakalász and Budakalász-Lenfonó), so confirm your stop before travelling.

name: Római Open-Air Bath
description: A summer-season open-air bath in Óbuda's Rómaifürdő district, on ground that once belonged to Roman Aquincum. The present layout dates from 1964 and was modernised around 2000, with a swimming pool, an adventure pool and several slides. The nearby Danube riverbank is a separate, newer public beach.

children.text: The Római Strandfürdő is an open-air bath at Rozgonyi Piroska utca 2 in Óbuda, in Budapest's 3rd district. It is a seasonal summer bath. The BKK listing for the bath describes a large green area in the former Aquincum territory, with a children's pool, a swimming pool and an adventure pool, and the operator's own site is named there for current information.

The bath's name and setting come from the area's past. The BKK listing says the Romans already regarded the local springs as sacred and that chronicles from the time of King Matthias mention a hospital here. These are statements from a listing page, not a full history, so they are best read as local tradition. Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part adds that the neighbourhood of Rómaifürdő sits beside springs where mills once operated in the early 19th century.

The layout seen today dates from a renovation. Programturizmus says the renewed bath opened in 1964 and has kept its layout since, and that in 2000 the three pools were modernised with filtered circulation. The main pool became an adventure pool with a slide, neck showers and bubble jets, and the children's pool became a playground. The slides described include a rafting slide, a steep straight slide, a combined fast-and-winding slide and a family slide that several people can use together.

Do not confuse the bath with the Danube riverbank. According to Telex, a free public Danube beach at Római-part opened in 2021, the first legal one since 1973, but swimming was not allowed there at the time and only wading was; check the posted rules for the current season. Hungarian Wikipedia says the riverside area was once dominated by boathouses and company holiday resorts. The H5 HÉV line has a stop at Rómaifürdő, the closest rail link named in the sources, though they do not give the walking route.
Good to know
The H5 Szentendre HÉV stops at Rómaifürdő and Aquincum, according to Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part; check the walking route before you go.
The bath is seasonal, so check the operator's site for current dates, opening times and tickets.
The Danube riverside beach at Római-part is a separate, seasonal site run by the Óbuda district with its own rules on bathing, so check the notices on site before going in.

historyIntro: The Római open-air bath stands in Óbuda on ground that belonged to the Roman town of Aquincum. The documented history the sources give is of a bath renewed in 1964 and modernised in 2000, with older claims best read as tradition.

historySections.heading: Springs, mills and an old claim

children.text: The BKK listing for the bath says that the Romans already regarded the local springs as sacred and that chronicles from the time of King Matthias mention a hospital here. The listing does not cite a source for either statement, so they are best read as local tradition. Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Római-part is more specific about the early 19th century: the neighbourhood of Rómaifürdő lies beside springs where mills once operated, and the riverside was then a popular centre of river life with water clean enough for swimming.

Programturizmus states that the renovated Római Strandfürdő opened in 1964 and that it has kept the layout it had then. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that free public beaches on the Danube bank here, named Hungária, Duna and Tungsram, operated in the early 20th century, and that the official bathing places on the river were closed in 1973 because water quality had declined. The Római-part Danube beach, where swimming is not permitted, was opened by the district in 2021.

Programturizmus records that in 2000 the three pools of the bath were modernised and fitted with filtered circulation. The main pool became an adventure pool with a slide, neck showers and bubble jets, and the children's pool became a playground. The bath is an open-air, seasonal summer facility, and a 2025 news report named it among the bathing places that closed at the end of the season on 31 August.
